summary: Devices need automation to show what software they run, whether it has known vulnerabilities, and what suppliers recommend. This document extends the Manufacturer Usage Description (MUD) YANG schema with a transparency schema. The schema gives locations of software bills of materials (SBOMs) and vulnerability information.

eli5.summary: A cereal box lists its ingredients. This gives gadgets a way to say where to find the list of parts inside their software, and where to look for known problems.

questions: how devices report software bill of materials
where is the well-known sbom endpoint
subtitle: A small YANG extension to MUD that tells tools where to find a device's SBOM and vulnerability information.

tldr.problem: Operators need automation to find out what software a device runs, whether it has known vulnerabilities and what the supplier recommends, across tens of thousands of devices.
tldr.mechanism: A new 'transparency' extension to the MUD YANG model lists where to get an SBOM (a URL, the device's own well-known /.well-known/sbom, or a contact) and where to get vulnerability information. It points to the data and does not carry it.
tldr.outcome: Management tools can discover SBOM and vulnerability sources in a uniform way, and either kind of information is optional.

today: RFC 9472 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2023, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it. It extends the MUD model of RFC 8520.

sections.title: Finding SBOMs and Vulnerability Information
sections.content:
The RFC aims to answer two questions for large numbers of devices: is this system susceptible to a particular vulnerability, and which devices in an environment contain vulnerabilities that need action? A software bill of materials (SBOM) describes what software, with versions and dependencies, a device contains. Formats named in the RFC include SPDX and CycloneDX. Vulnerability information may use CycloneDX, CVRF or CSAF.

This memo does not specify those formats, nor how to get vulnerability information directly from the endpoint. It only defines how to locate and retrieve the objects. The model is for discovery and gives no access to the underlying data. Either SBOM, vulnerability information or both can be provided.
sections.eli5: This does not hold the ingredient list itself. It is a signpost that says where the list is kept.

sections.title: Where the Information Lives
sections.content:
Two use cases drive the design: a network-layer management system retrieving information from an Internet of Things device, and an application-layer management system evaluating the posture of an application server. The RFC says objects may be found in one of three ways:

  • on the device itself, for example via an HTTP or CoAP endpoint;
  • on a website, via a URI that is discovered through MUD, DHCP or bootstrapping mechanisms;
  • through out-of-band contact with the supplier, who may evaluate each request and answer with the SBOM, the vulnerability information, a restricted URL or no access.

For application-layer discovery the RFC defines a well-known URI, /.well-known/sbom, which retrieves an SBOM. The pointer to a MUD file can be shared by the mechanisms of RFC 8520, in documentation or in a QR code on a box. MUD's cache-validity node lets manufacturers control how often tools recheck, which matters because SBOM and vulnerability data change at different rates.
sections.eli5: The list might be inside the gadget, on the maker's website, or you might have to phone the maker and ask.

sections.title: Formats and Content Types
sections.content:
Because many formats exist, tools must look at the Content-Type header of the response to see which one they received. Constrained devices are poor at content negotiation, so using an Accept header in HTTP or the Accept Option in CoAP is NOT RECOMMENDED. Backend tooling is encouraged to support all known formats and SHOULD silently discard SBOM information sent with a media type it does not understand.

Some formats carry both software inventory and vulnerability data. If both come from the same URL, both sbom-url and the matching vuln-url entry MUST indicate that, and network management systems MUST NOT fetch the same resource a second time.
sections.eli5: Lists come in different styles, so the label on the package says which style it is. Your tool just skips styles it cannot read.

sections.title: The mud-transparency Extension
sections.content:
The extension is named transparency and is listed in the extensions array of the MUD file. The YANG module ietf-mud-transparency then augments the mud container with a transparency container. The grouping can also be used independently of MUD.

SBOM location is a choice of three cases: sboms, a list keyed by version-info where each entry has an sbom-url (coap, coaps, http or https); sbom-local-well-known, naming the protocol to use against the device; or sbom-contact-uri, a tel, http, https or mailto URI for contacting someone. An optional sbom-archive-list URI returns a JSON list of previously published SBOMs. Vulnerability information is a choice between a list of vuln-url entries and a vuln-contact-uri.

The module defines identities for the local protocol choice: http and coap are NOT RECOMMENDED because they are insecure, while https and coaps are the secure options.
sections.eli5: It is a form with blanks: 'SBOM is at this address', 'ask this person', and 'known problems are listed here'. You fill in only the blanks you need.

sections.title: Example MUD Files
sections.content:
Section 5 of the RFC gives four example MUD files. The first points to both an SBOM and vulnerability information in the cloud, and then shows an SBOM-only variant. The second has the SBOM on the device with sbom-local-well-known set to https, first with no vulnerability information and then with vulnerability information in the cloud. The RFC notes this mixed case is likely common because vendors may learn of vulnerabilities more often than they update software. The third needs further contact before the SBOM can be obtained. The fourth adds access control lists, which are not required but described as a very good idea for IP-based devices.

With a file like that, the management system can GET the SBOM, read the Content-Type to learn the format, repeat the process for vulnerability information, and apply the ACLs.
sections.eli5: The examples are sample forms already filled in, so you can see what a finished one looks like.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module only helps discover information and has no operational impact on the device. The RFC notes unencrypted retrieval allows manipulation, so implementations are RECOMMENDED to offer a way to configure TLS or DTLS. If an attacker changes the locations, automation could fetch false information or URLs pointing to malware. Suggested defenses are testing cloud URLs against a reputation service and letting an administrator approve processing when the authority changes to one not known to be reputable.

An SBOM can help an attacker pick an exploit, so an endpoint SHOULD NOT give unrestricted access to the well-known URL by default. Other servers MAY restrict access using HTTP authorization, for example client certificates issued after registration, or OAuth. A client that is not authorized MUST get an error with instructions on how to register. Skew between the published SBOM and the software actually on a device can lead to the wrong policy, and a unique mapping of software version to SBOM reduces that. Manufacturers SHOULD recommend network access controls.
sections.eli5: A list of parts can also help a burglar find the weak lock, so the maker should only show it to people who have a good reason to ask.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA added transparency to the MUD Extensions registry and registered the YANG module ietf-mud-transparency, with namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-mud-transparency and prefix mudtx. It also added the well-known URI suffix sbom with the status permanent.
sections.eli5: The name tags the new feature uses were written in the official list so nobody else grabs them.
